newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechnya war leaves huge scar on Russia.
newsitem.headline: Chechnya war leaves huge scar on Russia.

text.p: Two years ago on Wednesday President Boris Yeltsin sent thousands of Russian troops, backed by tanks and combat planes, into tiny breakaway Chechnya to "restore constitutional order".

Now the last servicemen are trickling out of the North Caucasus region, leaving behind thousands of dead comrades, tens of thousands of dead civilians and a devastated land firmly controlled by the separatists they had come to crush.
The West has welcomed the end of the war and thousands of Russian families are happy that their sons no longer risk being killed in the unpopular conflict.

But the political and military humiliation of the Kremlin at the hands of the lightly-armed but determined Chechen rebels is evident, although some analysts say that Yeltsin has won political and possibly economic capital by ending the conflict.
Sergei Markov, political analyst with the Carnegie Endownment for International Peace think-tank, said the situation now was much worse than before the Russian troops moved into Chechnya.
"The crisis of Russia's statehood has only deepened," he said. "The armed forces are demoralised, the organs of state power are demoralised," he said.

Markov said there would be a syndrome developing in Russia similar to the "Vietnam syndrome" in the United States, where the military loss in a foreign land resulted in a national wariness toward the military and foreign involvement.
Also thousands of U.S. veterans found themselves crippled, both morally and physically after the war in Vietnam and the consequences are still felt.
On the face of it, Russia has left Chechnya entirely to the separatists.

Aslan Maskhadov, who led the Chechen military resistance which humiliated Russian forces, is now not only recognised by Moscow as prime minister but is the man it would like to see elected president in a regional poll on January 27.

One of his ministers and another presidential candidate is Shamil Basayev, who led a raid into Russia proper in 1995, taking thousands of people hostage in a hospital. Some 140 people were killed in the raid and a clash with Russian troops.

A third minister and would-be president is Movladi Udugov, who, armed with a sattelite telephone, has practically single-handedly won the propaganda war against the Kremlin and now takes part in most of the talks with Russian delegations.

Only Dzhokar Dudayev, the Soviet general who spearheaded Chechnya's independence drive since 1991, is not there. He was reported killed in April in what the separatists called a targeted Russian missile attack.
The turnaround in Yeltsin's policy on Chechnya -- from "no talks with the bandits" to "withdrawal of troops and talks are the only solution" has been dramatic.

The Russian leader has admitted that the decision to send troops into Chechnya could have been his biggest mistake in his life but has not gone any further or explained why he had taken the decision and why he has since changed his mind.
Markov said that paradoxically both decisions -- to start the war and to end it -- were explained by Yeltsin's desire to strengthen his power.

"He is capable of sending troops to enhance his power and he may pull them out to achieve the same goal," he said, in a clear reference to the role played by the search for a political solution in helping Yeltsin to win the presidential election.
"We are marking the fifth anniversary of the break-up of the Soviet Union now and Yeltsin's role in it to a certain extent was also motivated by a striving for power," he said.

But Lev Bruni, deputy editor of the liberal Sevodnya newspaper, said Russia may also gain economically from a peaceful settlement in Chechnya, through which Caspian oil from Azerbaijan is due to be transported to the port of Novorossiisk.
"A certain economic clarity has emerged and the two sides are close to an agreement on sharing profits," Bruni said.

After initial outrage, public reaction to the Chechnya conflict was muted. Bruni said that was due to a multitude of problems facing Russians during their country's chaotic transition to a market economy.
"It was just one of the problems, not the biggest problem."
